title: Cocaine-induced MI with hypokalemia: intracellular potassium shift
vignette: A 44-year-old man comes to the hospital due to acute onset of central chest pain radiating to the left arm. He used cocaine a few hours ago. Blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg, pulse is 98/min, and respirations are 18/min. On examination, the patient appears anxious and diaphoretic. Electrocardiogram shows ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads. Laboratory studies reveal an elevated cardiac troponin level and a serum potassium concentration of 3.1 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypokalemia?

clues.text: used cocaine a few hours ago
clues.note: Cocaine causes a surge in catecholamines (blocks reuptake). Excess catecholamines drive potassium INTO cells via beta-2-adrenergic stimulation of the Na/K-ATPase - producing acute hypokalemia.

clues.text: ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads
clues.note: ST elevation with elevated troponin indicates an acute myocardial infarction (cocaine-induced coronary vasospasm/thrombosis) - a major physiologic stress amplifying catecholamine release.
Hypokalemia (K+ 3.1 / normal 3.5-5.0 mEq/L). With total body potassium unchanged acutely, the low serum level reflects an intracellular SHIFT driven by catecholamines - not renal or GI loss.

whatMatters: Cocaine + acute MI = massive catecholamine (beta-adrenergic) surge, which activates the Na/K-ATPase and shifts potassium INTO cells. That intracellular shift lowers serum K+ (3.1 / normal 3.5-5.0) acutely without a change in total body potassium. Answer C. (Not renal or GI loss.)
strategy: Ask WHERE the potassium went. Acute hypokalemia with a catecholamine surge (cocaine/stress/MI, or beta-agonists, insulin, alkalosis) = intracellular SHIFT (answer C), not a true loss. Reject loss mechanisms (renal/GI) and 'new cell uptake' (which needs rapid hematopoiesis, e.g., leukemia/GM-CSF, not present here).

options.text: Exchange of potassium with sodium in the intestine
Increased use of potassium by new cells

eliminations.label: Decreased dietary intake - too slow/severe
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: hypokalemia from very poor oral intake (anorexia, starvation). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: dietary lack develops slowly and doesn't explain acute hypokalemia during a catecholamine surge. ✅ Correct if: chronic malnutrition/anorexia.

eliminations.label: Intestinal K/Na exchange - GI cation exchangers
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: GI potassium loss (e.g., cation-exchange resins, diarrhea). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: no GI losses are described; the cause here is a transcellular shift. ✅ Correct if: prolonged diarrhea or a potassium-binding resin.

eliminations.label: Increased urinary loss - hyperaldosteronism/diuretics, your pick
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: renal potassium wasting from diuretics or elevated aldosterone. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: nothing indicates diuretics or hyperaldosteronism; this patient's hypertension is from cocaine, and the acute drop reflects an intracellular shift. ✅ Correct if: diuretic use or primary hyperaldosteronism.

eliminations.label: Increased use by new cells - rapid hematopoiesis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: potassium uptake during accelerated cell production (acute leukemia, GM-CSF, B12 treatment of megaloblastic anemia). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those risk factors aren't present. ✅ Correct if: hypokalemia during rapid cell proliferation.

reasoning: Cocaine + acute MI -> large catecholamine (beta-adrenergic) surge
Beta-2 stimulation activates Na/K-ATPase, driving potassium INTO cells
Serum potassium falls acutely (3.1 mEq/L) without a change in total body potassium
-> increased intracellular shift of potassium; answer C
mechanism: Serum potassium can fall from decreased intake, renal or GI losses, or a transcellular SHIFT of potassium into cells. Severe physiologic stress (myocardial infarction) and cocaine both markedly increase circulating catecholamines (cocaine blocks catecholamine reuptake). Epinephrine/norepinephrine stimulate beta-2 adrenergic receptors, activating the Na/K-ATPase (and the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter) to move potassium INTRACELLULARLY; adrenergic activity also releases insulin, which further shifts potassium into cells. The result is acute hypokalemia (here 3.1 mEq/L) with total body potassium unchanged - a redistribution rather than a true loss. The same intracellular shift is seen with beta-agonist drugs (albuterol), insulin, and alkalosis. Renal/GI losses and uptake by rapidly dividing cells are the other categories, but none fit this acute catecholamine-driven scenario.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Renal/Physio > causes of hypokalemia: decreased intake, transcellular shift (beta-agonists, insulin, alkalosis, stress/catecholamines), renal loss (diuretics, hyperaldosteronism), GI loss.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: Classify the MECHANISM: acute catecholamine surge -> intracellular shift, not a true loss.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on transcellular shift, Na/K-ATPase, beta-2 adrenergic, or hypokalemia? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Increased urinary loss (your pick) needs diuretics/hyperaldosteronism (not present); GI loss and new-cell uptake also lack supporting clues.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: cocaine/stress/beta-agonists/insulin/alkalosis -> potassium shifts INTO cells -> acute hypokalemia (redistribution, not loss).

keywords.back: Activates Na/K-ATPase -> K+ into cells (lowers serum K)
Rapid hematopoiesis (acute leukemia, GM-CSF, B12 for megaloblastic anemia)
